summary: 1 Samuel 24 (22 verses) continues the story of kinghip. Starting with 'When Saul had returned from following the Philistines, he was told, “Behold, David is in the wilderness of En Gedi.”', it moves through themes of kinghip, prophet vs king and calls readers toward heart.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows kinghip lived out in transition to monarchy. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: When Saul had returned from following the Philistines, he was told, “Behold, David is in the wilderness of En Gedi.”
May Yahweh judge between me and you, and may Yahweh avenge me of you; but my hand will not be on you.
David swore to Saul. Saul went home, but David and his men went up to the stronghold.

questions.question: What is happening in 1 Samuel 24?
questions.answer: In 22 verses, this chapter 1 samuel 24 (22 verses) continues the story of kinghip. starting with 'when saul had returned from following the philistines, he was told, “behold, david is in the wilderness of en gedi.”', it moves through themes of kinghip, prophet vs king and calls readers toward heart. The setting is transition to monarchy, written to israel. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote 1 Samuel and why 24 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally samuel tradition, addressed to israel around ~1000 bc. This chapter fits the book's purpose as historical narrative — its themes of kinghip, prophet vs king build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'kingdom' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: God's reign/ rule. In this chapter, it appears in context of kinghip. For a first-time reader: think of it as god's reign/ rule, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through kinghip and prophet vs king, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 11 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'Moreover, my father, behold, yes, see the skirt of your robe in my hand; for in that I cut off the skirt of your robe and didn’t kill you, know and see that there is neither evil n...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about kinghip. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
